mcqs.question: What does BSG (Gut 2021) say should happen before investigating suspected iron deficiency anaemia?

options.B: Start oral iron and investigate only if it fails
options.C: Arrange bidirectional endoscopy for everyone straight away
options.D: Confirm iron deficiency with iron studies
options.E: Give a trial of IV iron

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Confirm iron deficiency with iron studies
mcqs.explanation: BSG 2021: iron deficiency should be confirmed by iron studies before investigation.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Iron deficiency should be confirmed by iron studies prior to investigation.

mcqs.question: According to BSG (2021), which is the single most useful marker of iron deficiency anaemia?
mcqs.explanation: Serum ferritin is the single most useful marker. Transferrin saturation helps if a false-normal ferritin is suspected.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Iron deficiency should be confirmed by iron studies prior to investigation. Serum ferritin is the single most useful marker of IDA, but other blood tests (eg, transferrin saturation) can be helpful if a false-normal ferritin is suspected.

mcqs.question: A patient with active inflammation might have a falsely normal ferritin. Which additional test does BSG (2021) suggest?
mcqs.explanation: BSG: other tests such as transferrin saturation can help if a false-normal ferritin is suspected.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Iron deficiency should be confirmed by iron studies prior to investigation. Serum ferritin is the single most useful marker of IDA, but other blood tests (eg, transferrin saturation) can be helpful if a false-normal ferritin is suspected.

mcqs.question: How does BSG (2021) define anaemia?

options.C: Hb below the lower limit for the population and lab
options.E: Hb below 100 g/L in all adults regardless of sex or age

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Hb below the lower limit for the population and lab
mcqs.explanation: BSG: anaemia is Hb below the lower limit of normal for the relevant population and the laboratory performing the test.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Anaemia should be defined as a haemoglobin (Hb) concentration below the lower limit of normal for the relevant population and laboratory performing the test.

mcqs.question: For which patients does BSG (2021) say the threshold for investigating non-anaemic iron deficiency should be low?

options.A: Men, postmenopausal women, GI symptoms or family history
options.D: Premenopausal women with heavy periods only

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Men, postmenopausal women, GI symptoms or family history
mcqs.explanation: BSG: low threshold for investigating NAID in men, postmenopausal women, and those with GI symptoms or a family history of GI pathology.

sourceRefs.excerpt: The threshold for investigation of non-anaemic iron deficiency should be low in men, postmenopausal women, and those with GI symptoms or a family history of GI pathology.
The threshold for investigation of non-anaemic iron deficiency (NAID) should be low in men, postmenopausal women, and those with GI symptoms or a family history of GI pathology.

mcqs.question: In the 2020 trial of preoperative IV iron given 10–42 days before elective major abdominal surgery in anaemic patients (PREVENTT), what was the main finding?

options.A: Shortened length of stay by 5 days
options.B: Not superior to placebo for transfusion
options.D: Halved the transfusion rate in the first 30 days

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Not superior to placebo for transfusion
mcqs.explanation: Preoperative IV iron wasn't superior to placebo in reducing the need for blood transfusion. Safety endpoints didn't differ.

sourceRefs.excerpt: There were no significant differences between the two groups for any of the prespecified safety endpoints. Interpretation Preoperative intravenous iron was not superior to placebo to reduce need for blood transfusion when administered to patients with anaemia 10-42 days before elective major abdominal surgery. options.B: Faster Hb rise; delayed or reduced ESA need
options.D: No difference in Hb response at any time point measured

mcqs.explanation: IV FCM quickly reached and maintained Hb and delayed or reduced the need for other anaemia management, including ESAs. No renal toxicity was seen.

mcqs.question: In patients with heart failure and iron deficiency, what effect did IV ferric carboxymaltose have on recurrent HF hospitalisation or CV death at 1 year (ESC 2026 meta-analysis)?
mcqs.explanation: IV FCM significantly reduced recurrent HF hospitalisation or CV death at 1 year (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.62–0.85) and over maximum follow-up (RR 0.80).

sourceRefs.excerpt: Intravenous ferric carboxymaltose (FCM) significantly reduced the composite of recurrent hospitalizations for heart failure (HHF) or cardiovascular (CV) death at 1-year (RR 0.73, 95% CI 0.62-0.85) and over maximum follow-up (RR 0.80, 95% CI 0.68-0.94) compared to control in patients with heart failure (HF) and iron deficiency (ID). Recurrent HHF was significantly reduced with FCM administration (1-year RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.57-0.84; complete follow-up RR 0.75, 95% CI 0.60-0.94).

mcqs.question: In HF patients with CKD, what did IV iron do to first HF hospitalisation or CV death (ESC 2026)?

options.D: Reduced it only in dialysis patients

mcqs.explanation: IV iron significantly reduced first HF hospitalisation or CV death (RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.72–0.86) in HF with CKD.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Intravenous (IV) iron therapy showed a significantly reduced incidence of first heart failure hospitalization or cardiovascular death (RR = 0.79, 95% CI: 0.72–0.86) and heart failure hospitalization or cardiovascular death (RR = 0.85, 95% CI: 0.75–0.98) in heart failure (HF) patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) compared with the control group, with significant improvements in relevant biomarkers.

options.A: IV iron causes IBD flares in all patients
options.B: Oral iron is better absorbed in IBD
options.C: IV iron is contraindicated in IBD
options.D: Iron deficiency is rare in IBD
options.E: Oral iron may worsen IBD symptoms

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Oral iron may worsen IBD symptoms
mcqs.explanation: Iron deficiency is common in IBD, and oral iron is suggested to exacerbate IBD symptoms, prompting a PO versus IV comparison.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Objective Iron deficiency is a common complication in patients with IBD and oral iron therapy is suggested to exacerbate IBD symptoms. mcqs.question: In IBD-associated anaemia, when does the 2014 Polish guidance suggest considering erythropoietin?

options.C: Hb <10 g/dl or IV iron failure after 4 weeks
options.E: Hb below 13 g/dl in any patient taking oral iron

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Hb <10 g/dl or IV iron failure after 4 weeks
mcqs.explanation: Consider erythropoietin if Hb is under 10 g/dl or high-dose IV iron has been unsuccessful after 4 weeks.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Erythropoietin administration should be considered in patients with haemoglobin less than 10 g/dl or in whom high dose intravenous iron therapy was unsuccessful (after 4 weeks of treatment).

mcqs.question: After a blood transfusion in IBD, what does the 2014 Polish guidance recommend?

options.A: Monitor and plan further parenteral iron
options.E: No further iron if Hb is normal, whatever the ferritin

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Monitor and plan further parenteral iron
mcqs.explanation: The patient should be monitored and further parenteral iron scheduled post transfusion, even if Hb is normal.

sourceRefs.excerpt: The patient should be monitored and further parenteral iron substitution scheduled post transfusion, even if haemoglobin level is normal.

mcqs.question: What does the Anemia (2025) review recommend for pregnant women with IDA?
mcqs.explanation: Pregnant women with IDA should receive iron supplementation, because IDA increases maternal morbidity, preterm delivery and low birthweight.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Pregnant women with IDA should receive iron supplementation, as IDA increases the likelihood of maternal morbidity, preterm delivery and low birth weight.

mcqs.question: Which tests does the Anemia (2025) review suggest for screening children for IDA?

options.A: FBC, or serum iron and ferritin
options.C: Stool calprotectin alone, without blood tests

mcqs.correctAnswerText: FBC, or serum iron and ferritin
mcqs.explanation: Use complete blood counts or serum iron and ferritin levels to screen for IDA in children.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Use complete blood counts or serum iron and ferritin levels to screen for IDA in children.

mcqs.question: Above what national anaemia prevalence do UNICEF, UNU and WHO jointly recommend starting anaemia screening?
mcqs.explanation: UNICEF, UNU and WHO jointly recommend initiating anaemia screening when a country's anaemia prevalence exceeds 5%.

sourceRefs.excerpt: UNICEF, UNU and WHO also jointly recommend initiating anaemia screening when a country’s anaemic prevalence exceeds 5%.

mcqs.question: Which iron compounds does the Anemia (2025) review prefer for food fortification?
mcqs.explanation: Water-soluble iron compounds are preferred because of their high solubility in gastric juices. High bioavailability with minimal sensory change is the priority.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Water‐soluble iron compounds, due to their high solubility in gastric juices, should be the preferred choice for food fortification.
Selection of iron compounds for food fortification should prioritise high bioavailability while minimising undesirable sensory alterations of food.

mcqs.question: Which risk factors does the Anemia (2025) review say universal anaemia screening in children should assess?
mcqs.explanation: Screening should include risk factors such as prematurity or low birthweight, lead exposure and prolonged exclusive breastfeeding.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Universal screening for anaemia should include a comprehensive assessment of risk factors for iron deficiency or IDA (e.g., prematurity, low birth weight, lead exposure, prolonged exclusive breastfeeding beyond 4 months without supplemental iron, or transition to whole milk/low-iron complementary foods).

mcqs.question: Which micronutrient pattern does WHO (2026) report in paediatric IDA?

options.D: Lower iron, zinc, Mg; higher copper
options.E: Higher iron and zinc, with lower magnesium levels

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Lower iron, zinc, Mg; higher copper
mcqs.explanation: Paediatric IDA is associated with lower iron, zinc and magnesium, and higher copper.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Pediatric iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is associated with significantly lower levels of iron, zinc, and magnesium, and higher levels of copper.

mcqs.question: Which approach does WHO (2026) describe as promising for nutritional interventions in pregnant women with IDA?

options.D: Routine IV iron for all pregnant women in the cohort

mcqs.explanation: mHealth-based nutritional interventions are promising for addressing implementation challenges in pregnant women with IDA.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Mobile health (mHealth)-based nutritional interventions are a promising alternative to address challenges in implementing nutritional interventions for iron deficiency anemia in pregnant women, such as limited healthcare access, poor adherence to supplementation, and gaps in nutrition knowledge and counseling.

mcqs.question: Which screening tests does the Anemia (2025) review recommend for countries with adequate to intermediate resources?

options.E: Bone marrow iron staining in every child

mcqs.explanation: Countries with adequate to intermediate resources are recommended to screen with haemoglobin and haematocrit tests.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Countries with adequate to intermediate levels of resources are recommended to screen for anaemia using haemoglobin and haematocrit tests.

mcqs.explanation: NICE (2019, amended 2025): refer people with CAP to hospital if symptoms aren't improving as expected with antibiotics.

mcqs.question: According to ACOG (2011), what constitutes a hypertensive emergency in pre-eclampsia or eclampsia?

options.B: Any BP above 140/90 on two separate clinic occasions
options.E: Severe BP (≥160/≥110) persisting 15 min or more

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Severe BP (≥160/≥110) persisting 15 min or more

mcqs.question: What BP target does the South African guideline (2011) set, and what about patients with end-organ damage?

options.B: <160/100 for everyone, whatever organ damage exists

mcqs.correctAnswerText: <140/90, with stricter control in organ damage
mcqs.explanation: Target systolic <140 and diastolic <90 mmHg, with stricter control required for patients with end-organ damage.

sourceRefs.excerpt: The target blood pressure for antihypertensive management is systolic <140 mmHg and diastolic <90 mmHg; however, stricter BP control is required for patients with end-organ damage, co-existing risk factors and co-morbidity (e.g., diabetes mellitus).

mcqs.question: Clinic BP is 165/100 mmHg with no target organ damage or red flags. What does NICE recommend to confirm the diagnosis?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: if clinic BP is between 140/90 and 180/120, offer ABPM to confirm the diagnosis.

sourceRefs.excerpt: If clinic blood pressure is between 140/90 mmHg and 180/120 mmHg, offer ambulatory blood pressure monitoring (ABPM) to confirm the diagnosis of hypertension. See the section on identifying who to refer for people with a clinic blood pressure 180/120 mmHg or higher. [2019]

topics.topicKey: lyme disease borrelia tick bite erythema migrans disseminated disease doxycycline
topics.topicDisplayName: Lyme disease: Borrelia, tick bite, erythema migrans, disseminated disease, doxycycline
topics.coverageNote: Merged with the duplicate Lyme topic (#75). The stored rows don't give antibiotic doses or durations (NICE tables 1–2 aren't stored), so no dosing questions.

mcqs.question: A walker asks about their risk after a tick bite. What does NICE say?

options.A: Ticks should be left in place for 24 hours
options.B: Most bites don't transmit Lyme; prompt removal helps
options.C: Serology should be done immediately after a bite
options.D: Prophylactic antibiotics are needed after all tick bites
options.E: Every tick bite transmits Lyme disease

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Most bites don't transmit Lyme; prompt removal helps
mcqs.explanation: NICE: most tick bites do not transmit Lyme disease, and prompt, correct removal of the tick reduces the risk of transmission.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Be aware that most tick bites do not transmit Lyme disease and that prompt, correct removal of the tick reduces the risk of transmission.

mcqs.question: An asymptomatic person had a tick bite last week. What does NICE advise?

options.E: Diagnose Lyme and treat for 21 days

mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not diagnose Lyme disease in people without symptoms, even if they have had a tick bite.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not diagnose Lyme disease in people without symptoms, even if they have had a tick bite.

mcqs.question: A patient has symptoms suggestive of Lyme disease but can't recall a tick bite. What's the NICE position?

options.A: Treat as an insect bite allergy
options.C: Test only if a tick is found
options.D: Lyme is excluded without a bite history

mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not rule out Lyme disease in people with symptoms but no clear history of tick exposure.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not rule out the possibility of Lyme disease in people with symptoms but no clear history of tick exposure.

mcqs.question: How does NICE say people without erythema migrans should be diagnosed?

options.A: Clinical picture alone in all cases, without any tests

mcqs.explanation: NICE: use clinical presentation and laboratory testing combined, and don't rule out diagnosis if tests are negative but suspicion is high.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Use a combination of clinical presentation and laboratory testing to guide diagnosis and treatment in people without erythema migrans. Do not rule out diagnosis if tests are negative but there is high clinical suspicion of Lyme disease.

mcqs.question: Lyme disease without erythema migrans is suspected. Which initial test does NICE recommend?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: offer an ELISA test, and consider starting antibiotics while awaiting results if clinical suspicion is high.

sourceRefs.excerpt: offer an enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) test for Lyme disease and
consider starting treatment with antibiotics while waiting for the results if there is a high clinical suspicion of Lyme disease.

mcqs.question: The immunoblot is negative but symptoms persist. What does NICE suggest?

options.A: Repeat the ELISA monthly until it becomes positive
options.B: Discussion with or referral to a specialist

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Discussion with or referral to a specialist
mcqs.explanation: NICE: if the immunoblot is negative (whatever the ELISA result) but symptoms persist, consider discussion with or referral to a specialist.

sourceRefs.excerpt: If the immunoblot test for Lyme disease is negative (regardless of the ELISA result) but symptoms persist, consider a discussion with or referral to a specialist, to: review whether further tests may be needed for suspected Lyme disease, for example, synovial fluid aspirate or biopsy, or lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid analysis or consider alternative diagnoses (both infectious, including other tick-borne diseases, and non-infectious diseases). Choose a specialist appropriate for the per

mcqs.question: A patient brings Lyme test results from an overseas private laboratory. What does NICE advise?

options.A: Treat on the basis of the private result alone
options.C: Use only accredited, validated, EQA-participating labs
options.D: Accept all results, including from non-accredited private labs

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Use only accredited, validated, EQA-participating labs
mcqs.explanation: NICE: don't routinely diagnose on tests done outside the NHS unless the lab is accredited, takes part in external quality assurance and uses validated tests.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not routinely diagnose Lyme disease based only on tests done outside the NHS, unless the laboratory used is accredited, participates in formal external quality assurance programmes and uses validated tests (see recommendation 1.2.22). If there is any doubt about tests: review the person's clinical presentation and carry out testing again using a UKAS-accredited laboratory and/or seek advice from a national reference laboratory.
use validated tests (validation should include published evidence on the test methodology, its relation to Lyme disease and independent reports of performance) and

mcqs.question: An adult with Lyme disease has focal neurological symptoms. What does NICE recommend?

options.A: Specialist discussion or referral without delaying treatment

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Specialist discussion or referral without delaying treatment
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider discussion with or referral to an appropriate specialist without delaying treatment.

sourceRefs.excerpt: If an adult with Lyme disease has focal symptoms, consider a discussion with or referral to a specialist, without delaying treatment. Choose a specialist appropriate for the person's symptoms, for example, an adult infection specialist, rheumatologist or neurologist.

mcqs.question: An adult with Lyme arthritis had doxycycline but treatment may have failed. What does NICE suggest?

options.B: A second course with an alternative, e.g. amoxicillin
options.C: Repeat doxycycline at a higher dose

mcqs.correctAnswerText: A second course with an alternative, e.g. amoxicillin
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider a second course using an alternative antibiotic, e.g. amoxicillin after an initial doxycycline course for Lyme arthritis.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider a second course of antibiotics for people with ongoing symptoms if treatment may have failed. Use an alternative antibiotic to the initial course, for example, for adults with Lyme disease and arthritis, offer amoxicillin if the person has completed an initial course of doxycycline.

mcqs.question: A patient has Lyme carditis. Which antibiotic does NICE advise against?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not use azithromycin in people with cardiac abnormalities associated with Lyme disease because of its effect on QT.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Note: Do not use azithromycin to treat people with cardiac abnormalities associated with Lyme disease because of its effect on QT interval.

mcqs.question: What three criteria does EFNS (2010) require for definite Lyme neuroborreliosis?

options.D: Neuro symptoms, CSF pleocytosis, intrathecal antibodies

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Neuro symptoms, CSF pleocytosis, intrathecal antibodies
mcqs.explanation: EFNS: definite LNB requires neurological symptoms, CSF pleocytosis and intrathecal Bb-specific antibodies. Possible LNB requires two of these.

sourceRefs.excerpt: For definite Lyme neuroborreliosis (LNB), three criteria should be fulfilled: neurological symptoms, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) pleocytosis, and Borrelia burgdorferi (Bb)-specific antibodies produced intrathecally. For possible LNB, two of these criteria should be met.

mcqs.question: Which feature isn't part of the low-risk 'Rule of 7's' for paediatric Lyme meningitis?
mcqs.explanation: Rule of 7's: low risk if headache <7 days, CSF mononuclear cells <70%, and no seventh or other cranial nerve palsy. Serology isn't one of the criteria.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Objectives The "Rule of 7's," a Lyme meningitis clinical prediction rule, classifies children at low risk for Lyme meningitis when each of the following 3 criteria are met: <7 days of headache, <70% cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) mononuclear cells, and absence of seventh or other cranial nerve pa

mcqs.question: How is Lyme arthritis diagnosed in children, according to German paediatric guidance (2012)?

options.A: History of a tick bite alone
options.B: New arthritis plus high-titre serum IgG
options.C: Joint fluid culture alone, without any serology result

mcqs.correctAnswerText: New arthritis plus high-titre serum IgG
mcqs.explanation: Lyme arthritis is diagnosed with newly recognised arthritis and high-titre serum IgG against B. burgdorferi.

sourceRefs.sourceBody: German Academy for Pediatrics and Adolescent Health
sourceRefs.excerpt: Lyme arthritis is diagnosed in the presence of newly recognized arthritis and high-titer serum IgG antibodies against B. burgdorferi.

mcqs.question: What did the 2003 trials of extended antibiotics for post-treatment Lyme symptoms show?

options.B: Marked cognitive improvement sustained for 6 months

mcqs.explanation: There were no significant differences between antibiotic and placebo groups, and no objective cognitive impairment without evidence of persisting infection.

sourceRefs.excerpt: However, there were no significant differences between those receiving antibiotics and placebo. Conclusion Patients with post-treatment chronic Lyme disease who have symptoms but show no evidence of persisting Borrelia infection do not show objective evidence of cognitive impairment.

mcqs.question: What does Infect Dis Now (2025) recommend when symptoms persist after appropriate Lyme treatment?

options.B: Prolonged antibiotics for several months without review

mcqs.explanation: Persistent symptoms after appropriate treatment require systematic reassessment of the initial diagnosis, adherence to and adequacy of treatment.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Persistent symptoms following appropriate treatment of confirmed Lyme borreliosis (LB) require a systematic clinical reassessment to verify the accuracy of the initial diagnosis, adherence to and adequacy of antibiotic therapy, and to consider potential sequelae or differential diagnoses.

mcqs.question: Fatigue, diffuse pain and cognitive symptoms persist after Lyme treatment with no alternative explanation. What label does Infect Dis Now (2025) suggest?

options.C: Chronic active Borrelia infection needing antibiotics

mcqs.explanation: Such symptoms may correspond to Post-Treatment Lyme Disease Syndrome when no alternative explanation is found.

sourceRefs.excerpt: When no alternative explanation is found for persistent symptoms after Lyme borreliosis treatment, and symptoms include fatigue, diffuse pain, and cognitive impairment, they may correspond to Post-Treatment Lyme Disease Syndrome (PTLDS).

mcqs.question: The history suggests re-infection with Lyme disease. What does NICE advise?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: if the history suggests re-infection, offer antibiotic treatment according to symptoms.

sourceRefs.excerpt: If the person's history suggests re‑infection, offer antibiotic treatment for Lyme disease according to their symptoms (see tables 1 and 2).

mcqs.question: A baby's mother was treated for Lyme disease in pregnancy, and the baby has Lyme-specific IgM. What does NICE advise?

options.D: Observe only, with repeat review at 12 months of age

mcqs.explanation: NICE: start treatment under specialist care if the baby has Lyme-specific IgM or there's any suspicion of infection.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Start treatment for Lyme disease under specialist care for babies of women treated for Lyme disease during pregnancy if the baby has IgM antibodies specific for Lyme disease or there is any suspicion the baby may be infected.

mcqs.question: Someone has an insect bite with no signs of infection. What does NICE advise about antibiotics?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not offer an antibiotic for an insect bite or sting in people without symptoms or signs of infection.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer an antibiotic for an insect bite or sting in people who do not have symptoms or signs of an infection.

mcqs.question: When should someone with an insect bite or sting be referred to hospital, according to NICE?

options.C: Signs of serious illness, e.g. systemic allergy

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Signs of serious illness, e.g. systemic allergy
mcqs.explanation: NICE: refer to hospital if there are signs of more serious illness, such as a systemic allergic reaction.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Refer people with an insect bite or sting to hospital if they have symptoms or signs suggesting a more serious illness or condition, such as a systemic allergic reaction (see the NICE guideline on anaphylaxis ).

mcqs.question: Which patients does NICE suggest prescribing less maintenance fluid to (e.g. 20–25 ml/kg/day)?

options.A: All young adults after surgery, regardless of comorbidity
options.B: Renal impairment, heart failure, older or frail

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Renal impairment, heart failure, older or frail
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider less fluid for older or frail patients, those with renal impairment or cardiac failure, and malnourished patients at risk of refeeding.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider prescribing less fluid (for example, 20 to 25 ml/kg/day fluid) for patients who: are older or frail; have renal impairment or cardiac failure; are malnourished and at risk of refeeding syndrome (see the NICE guideline on nutrition support in adults ).

mcqs.question: What routine maintenance regimen does NICE suggest considering on day 1?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider 25–30 ml/kg/day sodium chloride 0.18% in 4% glucose with 27 mmol/l potassium on day 1. More than 2.5 L/day increases hyponatraemia risk.

sourceRefs.excerpt: When prescribing for routine maintenance alone, consider using 25 to 30 ml/kg/day sodium chloride 0.18% in 4% glucose with 27 mmol/l potassium on day 1 (there are other regimens to achieve this). Prescribing more than 2.5 litres per day increases the risk of hyponatraemia. These are initial prescriptions and further prescriptions should be guided by monitoring. mcqs.question: A patient has had IV fluids with chloride above 120 mmol/l (e.g. 0.9% saline). What monitoring does NICE recommend?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: monitor serum chloride daily. If hyperchloraemia or acidaemia develops, reassess the prescription.

sourceRefs.excerpt: If patients have received IV fluids containing chloride concentrations greater than 120 mmol/l (for example, sodium chloride 0.9%), monitor their serum chloride concentration daily. If patients develop hyperchloraemia or acidaemia, reassess their IV fluid prescription and assess their acid–base status. Consider less frequent monitoring for patients who are stable.

mcqs.question: What should initial monitoring of patients on continuing IV fluids include, according to NICE?

options.D: Daily status, U&E, balance; weight twice weekly

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Daily status, U&E, balance; weight twice weekly
mcqs.explanation: NICE: at least daily reassessment of clinical fluid status, urea, creatinine and electrolytes, and fluid balance charts, with weight twice weekly.

sourceRefs.excerpt: All patients continuing to receive IV fluids need regular monitoring. This should initially include at least daily reassessments of clinical fluid status, laboratory values (urea, creatinine and electrolytes) and fluid balance charts, along with weight measurement twice weekly. Be aware that: Patients receiving IV fluid therapy to address replacement or redistribution problems may need more frequent monitoring. Additional monitoring of urinary sodium may be helpful in patients with high-volume g

mcqs.question: How does NICE say potassium should be provided in IV fluids?

options.B: Premixed bags rounded to common strengths
options.D: Added to bags on the ward by the prescribing doctor

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Premixed bags rounded to common strengths
mcqs.explanation: NICE: round weight-based potassium to the nearest common premixed fluids. Adding potassium to IV bags is dangerous.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Weight-based potassium prescriptions should be rounded to the nearest common fluids available (for example, a 67 kg person should have fluids containing 20 mmol and 40 mmol of potassium in a 24‑hour period). Potassium should not be added to IV fluid bags as this is dangerous.

mcqs.question: A patient is receiving IV fluid resuscitation. What reassessment does NICE recommend?

options.C: Daily weight only, with a fluid balance chart at 24 hours

mcqs.explanation: NICE: reassess using ABCDE, monitor RR, pulse, BP and perfusion continuously, and measure venous lactate and/or arterial pH and base excess.

sourceRefs.excerpt: If patients are receiving IV fluids for resuscitation, reassess the patient using the ABCDE approach (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure), monitor their respiratory rate, pulse, blood pressure and perfusion continuously, and measure their venous lactate levels and/or arterial pH and base excess according to guidance on advanced life support (Resuscitation Council UK, 2011).

mcqs.question: What does NICE say an IV fluid management plan should include?

options.D: The 24-hour prescription and a monitoring plan

mcqs.correctAnswerText: The 24-hour prescription and a monitoring plan
mcqs.explanation: NICE: the plan should include the fluid and electrolyte prescription over the next 24 hours and the assessment and monitoring plan, reviewed by an expert daily initially.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Patients should have an IV fluid management plan, which should include details of: the fluid and electrolyte prescription over the next 24 hours; the assessment and monitoring plan. Initially, the IV fluid management plan should be reviewed by an expert daily. IV fluid management plans for patients on longer-term IV fluid therapy whose condition is stable may be reviewed less frequently.

mcqs.question: Which consequences of mismanaged IV fluids does NICE say staff should be trained to recognise and prevent?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: training should cover recognising and preventing pulmonary oedema, peripheral oedema, volume depletion and shock.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Healthcare professionals should receive training and education about, and be competent in, recognising, assessing and preventing consequences of mismanaged IV fluid therapy, including: pulmonary oedema; peripheral oedema; volume depletion and shock.

mcqs.question: What does NICE advise about clear incidents of IV fluid mismanagement, such as inadvertent overload?

options.B: Document them only in the notes, without wider reporting
options.C: Report them through critical incident systems
options.E: Report them only if the patient dies

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Report them through critical incident systems
mcqs.explanation: NICE: report clear incidents of fluid mismanagement through standard critical incident reporting to encourage improved practice.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Clear incidents of fluid mismanagement (for example, unnecessarily prolonged dehydration or inadvertent fluid overload due to IV fluid therapy) should be reported through standard critical incident reporting to encourage improved training and practice (see the table on consequences of fluid mismanagement to be reported as critical incidents ).

mcqs.question: Who does NICE say hospitals should appoint to oversee IV fluid governance?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: hospitals should have an IV fluids lead responsible for training, governance, audit and review of prescribing and outcomes.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Hospitals should have an IV fluids lead, responsible for training, clinical governance, audit and review of IV fluid prescribing and patient outcomes.

mcqs.question: What may resuscitation with 6% hydroxyethyl starch (HES 130/0.4 and 130/0.42) increase, compared with other fluids (ICM 2013)?
mcqs.explanation: ICM 2013: resuscitation with 6% HES may increase the risk of death or treatment with renal replacement therapy.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Fluid resuscitation of acutely ill adults with 6% hydroxyethyl starch (HES 130/0.4 and 130/0.42) compared to other resuscitation fluids may increase the risk of death or treatment with renal replacement therapy (RRT).

mcqs.question: What problem with acute renal failure definitions did ADQI (2004) highlight?

options.C: A single universal definition already existed for all
options.E: No consensus definition in critical illness

mcqs.correctAnswerText: No consensus definition in critical illness
mcqs.explanation: ADQI 2004: there was no consensus definition of ARF in critically ill patients, hampering comparisons and consistent fluid strategies.

sourceRefs.excerpt: There is no consensus definition of acute renal failure (ARF) in critically ill patients, making comparisons and consistent fluid management strategies difficult.

mcqs.question: What did the 2000 randomised CVVH study investigate in critically ill patients with acute renal failure?

options.A: IHD versus peritoneal dialysis in critically ill adults

mcqs.explanation: The prospective RCT examined the impact of different ultrafiltration doses, since an adequate CVVH dose hadn't been defined.

mcqs.explanation: ARF requiring dialysis in critically ill patients is associated with 50–80% in-hospital mortality. IHD was then the worldwide standard RRT.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Background Acute renal failure (ARF) requiring dialysis in critically ill patients is associated with an in-hospital mortality rate of 50 to 80%. mcqs.question: What did the 2002 study hypothesise chest radiographs could help assess in critically ill patients?
mcqs.explanation: The study hypothesised that CXRs could help assess intravascular volume, since they quantify pulmonary oedema in ALI and blood volume in normal subjects.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Study objectives Fluid balance concerns occur daily in critically ill patients, complicated by difficulties assessing intravascular volume. Chest radiographs (CXRs) quantify pulmonary edema in acute lung injury (ALI) and total blood volume in normal subjects. We hypothesized that CXRs would

mcqs.question: For which roles is CRRT commonly used in ICU, according to Critical Care (2014)?
mcqs.explanation: CRRT is commonly used in ICUs to provide renal replacement and fluid management, including in patients on ECMO.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is commonly used in intensive care units (ICU) to provide renal replacement and fluid management in critically ill patients, including those on extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO).

mcqs.question: What does Digestive Endoscopy (2024) describe as the preferred approach for early Barrett's neoplasia?
mcqs.explanation: Endoscopic resection (EMR or ESD) is preferred for early Barrett's neoplasia to reduce the need for surgery.

sourceRefs.sourceBody: Digestive endoscopy : official journal of the Japan Gastroenterological Endoscopy Society
sourceRefs.excerpt: Endoscopic resection (EMR or ESD) is the preferred approach for treating early Barrett's neoplasia to reduce the need for surgical interventions.

mcqs.question: What does NICE recommend as first-line treatment for visible oesophageal lesions with high-grade dysplasia?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: offer endoscopic resection of visible lesions as first-line treatment for HGD.

mcqs.question: After endoscopic resection of HGD in Barrett's oesophagus, what does NICE recommend for the residual Barrett's segment?

options.B: Argon plasma coagulation of the resection site only

mcqs.explanation: NICE: offer endoscopic ablation of any residual Barrett's oesophagus after endoscopic resection for HGD (and for T1a adenocarcinoma).

Offer endoscopic ablation of any residual Barrett's oesophagus to people with T1a oesophageal adenocarcinoma after treatment with endoscopic resection.

mcqs.question: What's NICE first-line treatment for T1a oesophageal adenocarcinoma?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: offer endoscopic resection as first-line treatment for T1a oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer endoscopic resection as first-line treatment to people with T1a oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

mcqs.question: Which pre-resection staging test does NICE advise against for suspected T1a oesophageal adenocarcinoma?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not use EUS before endoscopic resection for staging suspected T1a adenocarcinoma. CT shouldn't be used before resection for suspected T1 either.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not use endoscopic ultrasonography (EUS) before endoscopic resection for staging suspected T1a oesophageal adenocarcinoma.
Do not use CT before endoscopic resection for staging suspected T1 oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

mcqs.question: What does NICE recommend for staging suspected T1N0 oesophageal cancer?
mcqs.explanation: NICE (2018): offer endoscopic mucosal resection for staging for people with suspected T1N0 oesophageal cancer.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer endoscopic mucosal resection for staging for people with suspected T1N0 oesophageal cancer. [2018]
Offer endoscopic resection for staging, to people with suspected stage 1 oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

mcqs.question: Histology of the endoscopic resection shows T1b oesophageal adenocarcinoma. What does NICE suggest for nodal staging?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider EUS for nodal staging in suspected or histologically diagnosed T1b adenocarcinoma.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider EUS for nodal staging, for people with suspected T1b oesophageal adenocarcinoma based on endoscopic appearances or diagnosed with T1b oesophageal adenocarcinoma based on histological examination of endoscopic resection specimens.

mcqs.question: What does NICE recommend after endoscopic treatment for Barrett's oesophagus with dysplasia?

options.D: Discharge to the GP after resection

mcqs.explanation: NICE: offer endoscopic follow-up after endoscopic treatment for Barrett's with dysplasia (and for stage 1 adenocarcinoma).

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer endoscopic follow-up to people who have received endoscopic treatment for Barrett's oesophagus with dysplasia.
Offer endoscopic follow-up to people who have received endoscopic treatment for stage 1 oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

mcqs.question: How does the AGA (2019) describe endoscopic submucosal dissection?

options.C: Mature technique for en bloc removal of larger lesions
options.D: Only for gastric cancer in Asia
options.E: Inferior to EMR in all cases

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Mature technique for en bloc removal of larger lesions
mcqs.explanation: AGA 2019: ESD is a mature technique enabling complete removal of lesions too large for en bloc EMR or otherwise unsuitable.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Best Practice Advice 1: Endoscopic submucosal dissection should be recognized as a mature endoscopic technique that enables complete removal of lesions that are too large for en bloc endoscopic mucosal resection or are at increased risk of containing cancer. Any degree of submucosal invasion caries an increased risk of lymph node metastasis and alternative/additional therapy should be considered.

mcqs.question: How does the 2021 Khirurgiia report compare ESD with EMR for colorectal tumours?

options.A: EMR always achieves en bloc resection

mcqs.explanation: ESD is more advisable than EMR regarding resection quality for colorectal tumours.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) is more advisable regarding resection quality compared to endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR) for colorectal tumors.

mcqs.question: What does Endoscopy (2026) say about prophylactic clipping after colorectal ESD?

options.B: Increases perforation and is therefore not advised
options.E: May reduce delayed bleeding and perforation

mcqs.correctAnswerText: May reduce delayed bleeding and perforation

sourceRefs.excerpt: Prophylactic clipping after colorectal endoscopic submucosal dissection may reduce the risk of adverse events such as delayed bleeding, postprocedural perforation, and postelectrocoagulation syndrome, but its preventive efficacy requires further assessment.

mcqs.question: In the 2016 study, what treatment combination safely eradicated Barrett's with HGD or early cancer?
mcqs.explanation: Focal endoscopic resection followed by radiofrequency ablation safely and effectively eradicates BO containing HGD and/or early cancer.

options.A: ESD as a diagnostic and staging tool
options.B: ESD versus surgery for long-term overall survival

mcqs.correctAnswerText: ESD as a diagnostic and staging tool
mcqs.explanation: The study evaluated the role of ESD as a potential diagnostic and staging tool in Barrett's neoplasia.

mcqs.question: People with stage 1 oesophageal adenocarcinoma need a treatment decision. What does NICE recommend?

options.A: Consultation to discuss resection vs oesophagectomy

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Consultation to discuss resection vs oesophagectomy
mcqs.explanation: NICE: offer a clinical consultation to discuss and evaluate options, including endoscopic resection or oesophagectomy.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer a clinical consultation to people with stage 1 oesophageal adenocarcinoma to discuss and evaluate the suitability of treatment options, including endoscopic resection or oesophagectomy.

mcqs.question: What surveillance interval does NICE recommend for long-segment (3 cm or longer) Barrett's oesophagus?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: high-resolution white light endoscopy with Seattle biopsies every 2–3 years for long-segment Barrett's; every 3–5 years for short-segment.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer high resolution white light endoscopic surveillance with Seattle protocol biopsies: every 2 to 3 years to people with long-segment (3 cm or longer) Barrett's oesophagus; every 3 to 5 years to people with short-segment (less than 3 cm) Barrett's oesophagus with intestinal metaplasia.

mcqs.question: Indefinite dysplasia of the oesophagus is diagnosed. What does NICE suggest?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider 6-monthly endoscopic surveillance with optimised acid-suppressant dosing.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider endoscopic surveillance at 6 monthly intervals with dose optimisation of acid-suppressant medication for people diagnosed with indefinite dysplasia of the oesophagus.

mcqs.question: A patient has short-segment Barrett's without intestinal metaplasia, confirmed at 2 endoscopies. What does NICE recommend?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not offer surveillance for short-segment (<3 cm) Barrett's without intestinal metaplasia confirmed at 2 endoscopies.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer endoscopic surveillance to people with short-segment (less than 3 cm) Barrett's oesophagus without intestinal metaplasia provided the diagnosis has been confirmed at 2 endoscopies.

mcqs.question: What does NICE recommend after radiotherapy for T1b oesophageal adenocarcinoma?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: offer endoscopic follow-up to people who have had radiotherapy for T1b oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer endoscopic follow-up to people who have received radiotherapy for T1b oesophageal adenocarcinoma.

mcqs.question: What was the 2017 US study of ESD in Barrett's early neoplasia designed to assess?

options.B: ESD versus surgery for early gastric cancer
options.E: Efficacy and safety of ESD in the West

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Efficacy and safety of ESD in the West
mcqs.explanation: The role of ESD in Barrett's early neoplasia wasn't well defined (mostly Asian/European data), so this study assessed its efficacy and safety.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Background and aims The role of endoscopic submucosal dissection (ESD) in Barrett's early neoplasia is not well defined, with most studies originating from Asia and Europe. We aimed to assess the efficacy, safety, and results of ESD in Barrett's esophagus (BE) with high-grade dysplasia (HGD)

mcqs.question: When does NICE say endoscopic ultrasound should be offered for oesophageal and GOJ cancer?

options.B: Only to tell T2 from T3
options.C: Routinely for all lesions before any treatment
options.E: Only when it'll guide ongoing management

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Only when it'll guide ongoing management
mcqs.explanation: NICE (2018): offer EUS only if it will help guide ongoing management; don't use it only to distinguish T2 from T3.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer endoscopic ultrasound to people with oesophageal and gastro-oesophageal junction cancer only if it will help guide ongoing management. [2018]
Do not offer endoscopic ultrasound only to distinguish between T2 to T3 tumours in people with oesophageal and gastro-oesophageal junction tumours. [2018]

mcqs.question: When does NICE say liquid soap and water must be used instead of alcohol handrub?

options.B: Only at the start of a shift
options.C: Visibly soiled hands or possible C. difficile
options.E: Before every patient contact, even if hands look clean

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Visibly soiled hands or possible C. difficile
mcqs.explanation: NICE: use soap and water when hands are visibly soiled or potentially contaminated with body fluids, or where alcohol-resistant organisms such as C. difficile may spread.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Decontaminate hands preferably with a handrub (conforming to the British standard BS EN 1500:2013 [current at time of publication, March 2012]), except in the following circumstances, when liquid soap and water must be used: when hands are visibly soiled or potentially contaminated with body fluids or in clinical situations where there is potential for the spread of alcohol-resistant organisms (such as Clostridium difficile or other organisms that cause diarrhoeal illness). [new 2012].

mcqs.question: Which moments does NICE list for hand decontamination?

options.A: Only at the end of a ward round
options.C: Before/after contact, after body fluids or surroundings

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Before/after contact, after body fluids or surroundings
mcqs.explanation: NICE: immediately before and after every episode of direct contact or care, after body fluid exposure, after contact with surroundings, and after removing gloves.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Hands must be decontaminated in all of the following circumstances: immediately before every episode of direct patient contact or care, including aseptic procedures; immediately after every episode of direct patient contact or care; immediately after any exposure to body fluids; immediately after any other activity or contact with a patient's surroundings that could potentially result in hands becoming contaminated; immediately after removal of gloves. [new 2012].

mcqs.question: What does 'bare below the elbow' mean in NICE guidance?

options.C: No false nails, polish, watch or stoned rings; short sleeves
options.D: Long sleeves buttoned at the wrist

mcqs.correctAnswerText: No false nails, polish, watch or stoned rings; short sleeves
mcqs.explanation: NICE: bare below the elbow means no false nails, nail polish, wristwatch or stoned rings, and short sleeves or sleeves that can be rolled up.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Healthcare workers should ensure that their hands can be decontaminated throughout the duration of clinical work by: being bare below the elbow when delivering direct patient care (for the purposes of this guideline, bare below the elbow means: not wearing false nails, nail polish, a wristwatch or stoned rings; wearing short-sleeved garments or being able to roll or push up sleeves); removing wrist and hand jewellery; making sure that fingernails are short, clean and free of nail polish; coverin

mcqs.question: How long does NICE say hands should be rubbed together during handwashing?

options.D: At least 2 minutes for every application

mcqs.explanation: NICE: handwashing has three stages (preparation, washing and rinsing, drying), with vigorous rubbing for a minimum of 10–15 seconds.

sourceRefs.excerpt: An effective handwashing technique involves three stages: preparation, washing and rinsing, and drying. Preparation requires wetting hands under tepid running water before applying liquid soap or an antimicrobial preparation. The handwash solution must come into contact with all of the surfaces of the hand. The hands must be rubbed together vigorously for a minimum of 10–15 seconds, paying particular attention to the tips of the fingers, the thumbs and the areas between the fingers. Hands should

mcqs.question: Which technique does NICE describe for alcohol handrub?

options.B: All surfaces, especially tips, thumbs and webs, until dry
options.C: Rub, then dry with a towel immediately
options.D: Use it on visibly soiled hands
options.E: A quick wipe of the palms only

mcqs.correctAnswerText: All surfaces, especially tips, thumbs and webs, until dry
mcqs.explanation: NICE: hands should be free of dirt. Rub all surfaces vigorously, especially fingertips, thumbs and between the fingers, until the solution has evaporated.

sourceRefs.excerpt: When decontaminating hands using an alcohol handrub, hands should be free from dirt and organic material. The handrub solution must come into contact with all surfaces of the hand. The hands must be rubbed together vigorously, paying particular attention to the tips of the fingers, the thumbs and the areas between the fingers, until the solution has evaporated and the hands are dry. [2003]

mcqs.question: When does NICE say gloves must be worn?

options.D: Invasive procedures, sterile sites, broken skin, fluid risk
options.E: Only when hands are visibly dirty

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Invasive procedures, sterile sites, broken skin, fluid risk
mcqs.explanation: NICE: gloves must be worn for invasive procedures, contact with sterile sites, non-intact skin or mucous membranes, and activities risking exposure to blood or body fluids.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Gloves must be worn for invasive procedures, contact with sterile sites and non-intact skin or mucous membranes, and all activities that have been assessed as carrying a risk of exposure to blood, body fluids, secretions or excretions, or to sharp or contaminated instruments.

mcqs.question: How does NICE say gloves should be used?

options.B: Kept on for the whole shift
options.C: Washed with soap and reused for the same patient's care
options.D: Single-use, changed between patients and tasks

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Single-use, changed between patients and tasks
mcqs.explanation: NICE: gloves are single-use, put on immediately before contact and removed as soon as the activity is completed; change between patients and between activities.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Gloves must be worn as single-use items. They must be put on immediately before an episode of patient contact or treatment and removed as soon as the activity is completed. Gloves must be changed between caring for different patients, and between different care or treatment activities for the same patient. [2003]

mcqs.question: What does NICE recommend before manipulating a patient's urinary catheter?

options.B: Hand hygiene, then new clean non-sterile gloves
options.C: Wear the same gloves as for the last patient
options.E: Alcohol rub to the catheter and the same gloves as before

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Hand hygiene, then new clean non-sterile gloves
mcqs.explanation: NICE: decontaminate hands and wear a new pair of clean, non-sterile gloves before manipulating the catheter, and decontaminate hands after removing gloves.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Healthcare workers must decontaminate their hands and wear a new pair of clean, non-sterile gloves before manipulating a patient's catheter, and must decontaminate their hands after removing gloves. [2003]

mcqs.question: What does NICE say about bladder instillations or washouts to prevent catheter-associated infection?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: bladder instillations or washouts must not be used to prevent catheter-associated infections.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Bladder instillations or washouts must not be used to prevent catheter-associated infections. [2003]

mcqs.question: When does NICE say aseptic technique should be used?

options.C: Only for central lines and other long-term vascular access

mcqs.explanation: NICE: aseptic technique should be used during any clinical procedure that bypasses the body's natural defences.

sourceRefs.excerpt: An aseptic technique ensures that only uncontaminated equipment and fluids come into contact with susceptible body sites. It should be used during any clinical procedure that bypasses the body's natural defences. Using the principles of asepsis minimises the spread of organisms from one person to another.

mcqs.question: Which preoperative measure does NICE suggest considering where Staph. aureus is a likely cause of SSI?

options.E: Nasal mupirocin with chlorhexidine body wash

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Nasal mupirocin with chlorhexidine body wash
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider nasal mupirocin with chlorhexidine body wash before procedures where S. aureus is a likely cause of SSI, determined locally.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider nasal mupirocin in combination with a chlorhexidine body wash before procedures in which Staphylococcus aureus is a likely cause of a surgical site infection. This should be locally determined and take into account: the type of procedure; individual patient risk factors; the increased risk of side effects in preterm infants (see the recommendation on risks in babies in the section on antiseptic skin preparation ); the potential impact of infection. [2019]

mcqs.question: Which suture type does NICE suggest considering to reduce SSI, especially in paediatric surgery?
mcqs.explanation: NICE (2019): consider antimicrobial triclosan-coated sutures, especially in paediatric surgery.

sourceRefs.excerpt: When using sutures, consider using antimicrobial triclosan-coated sutures, especially for paediatric surgery, to reduce the risk of surgical site infection. [2019]

mcqs.question: What's NICE's position on routine hair removal to reduce surgical site infection?

options.A: Shave in theatre with a razor
options.E: Remove hair from a 20 cm area

mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not use hair removal routinely to reduce SSI risk.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not use hair removal routinely to reduce the risk of surgical site infection. [2008]

mcqs.question: What's NICE's position on mechanical bowel preparation to reduce SSI?

options.A: Use it for all abdominal surgery
options.B: Combine it with oral antibiotics for all
options.D: Use it for all colorectal surgery

mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not use mechanical bowel preparation routinely to reduce SSI risk.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not use mechanical bowel preparation routinely to reduce the risk of surgical site infection. [2008]

mcqs.question: How does NICE say the operating team should prepare hands before the first operation on a list?

options.A: No preparation if gloves are worn
options.E: Aqueous antiseptic solution with a single-use nail brush

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Aqueous antiseptic solution with a single-use nail brush
mcqs.explanation: NICE: wash hands before the first operation with an aqueous antiseptic surgical solution, using a single-use brush or pick for the nails.

sourceRefs.excerpt: The operating team should wash their hands prior to the first operation on the list using an aqueous antiseptic surgical solution, with a single-use brush or pick for the nails, and ensure that hands and nails are visibly clean. [2008]

mcqs.question: Before subsequent operations on a list, how should hands be prepared, according to NICE?

options.B: Full scrub with a brush before every single operation
options.D: Alcoholic rub or antiseptic surgical solution

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Alcoholic rub or antiseptic surgical solution
mcqs.explanation: NICE: before subsequent operations, use either an alcoholic hand rub or an antiseptic surgical solution; rewash if soiled.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Before subsequent operations, hands should be washed using either an alcoholic hand rub or an antiseptic surgical solution. If hands are soiled then they should be washed again with an antiseptic surgical solution. [2008]

mcqs.question: Which debridement methods does NICE advise against in managing surgical site infection?

options.A: Surgical debridement in theatre for every surgical wound
options.B: Eusol and gauze, dextranomer or enzymatic

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Eusol and gauze, dextranomer or enzymatic
mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not use Eusol and gauze, dextranomer or enzymatic treatments for debridement in SSI.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not use Eusol and gauze, or dextranomer or enzymatic treatments for debridement in the management of surgical site infection. [2008]

mcqs.question: What does NICE say about in-line filters for IV infusions?

options.D: Mandatory for all infusions, changed every 24 hours

mcqs.explanation: NICE: in-line filters should not be used routinely for infection prevention.

sourceRefs.excerpt: In-line filters should not be used routinely for infection prevention. [2003]

mcqs.question: What does Infect Dis Health (2023) emphasise for people with cystic fibrosis?

options.C: Cohort all PwCF together in a shared bay or clinic

mcqs.explanation: Avoiding cross-infection is critically important to prevent transmission of CF-related pathogens between people with CF.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Avoidance of cross-infection is critically important to prevent the transmission of cystic fibrosis (CF)-related microbial pathogens to persons/people with cystic fibrosis (PwCF).

mcqs.question: What does NICE recommend before discharging patients with intermittent catheters?

options.A: Teach hand hygiene, insertion and catheter care
options.E: Provide a leaflet only, with no hands-on demonstration

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Teach hand hygiene, insertion and catheter care
mcqs.explanation: NICE: patients and carers should be educated in hand decontamination, insertion of intermittent catheters where applicable, and catheter management before discharge.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Patients and carers should be educated about and trained in techniques of hand decontamination, insertion of intermittent catheters where applicable, and catheter management before discharge from hospital. [2003]

mcqs.question: A patient has a provoked DVT and the provoking factor has resolved, with an uncomplicated course. When does NICE suggest considering stopping anticoagulation?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider stopping 3 months after a provoked DVT/PE (3–6 months with active cancer) if the provoking factor has gone and the course was uncomplicated.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider stopping anticoagulation treatment 3 months (3 to 6 months for people with active cancer) after a provoked DVT or PE if the provoking factor is no longer present and the clinical course has been uncomplicated. If anticoagulation treatment is stopped, give advice about the risk of recurrence and provide: written information on symptoms and signs to look out for; direct contact details of a healthcare professional or team with expertise in thrombosis who can discuss any new symptoms or si

mcqs.question: After an unprovoked PE, what does NICE suggest about anticoagulation beyond 3 months?

options.D: Consider continuing, balancing recurrence and bleeding

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Consider continuing, balancing recurrence and bleeding
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider continuing beyond 3 months (6 months in active cancer) after unprovoked DVT/PE, based on recurrence versus bleeding risk and preferences.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider continuing anticoagulation beyond 3 months (6 months for people with active cancer) after an unprovoked DVT or PE . Base the decision on the balance between the person's risk of VTE recurrence and their risk of bleeding. Discuss the risks and benefits of long-term anticoagulation with the person, and take their preferences into account. [2020]

mcqs.question: Which bleeding risk tool does NICE suggest for people on anticoagulation for unprovoked proximal DVT or PE?

options.B: HAS-BLED; discuss stopping if ≥4 and unmodifiable

mcqs.correctAnswerText: HAS-BLED; discuss stopping if ≥4 and unmodifiable
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider HAS-BLED. Discuss stopping anticoagulation if the score is 4 or more and can't be modified.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider using the HAS-BLED score for major bleeding risk to assess the risk of major bleeding in people having anticoagulation treatment for unprovoked proximal DVT or PE. Discuss stopping anticoagulation if the HAS-BLED score is 4 or more and cannot be modified. [2020]

mcqs.question: What does NICE say about predictive risk tools for deciding on long-term anticoagulation?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not rely solely on predictive risk tools to assess the need for long-term anticoagulation.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not rely solely on predictive risk tools to assess the need for long-term anticoagulation treatment. [2020]

mcqs.question: Which anticoagulant does NICE suggest considering for people with active cancer and confirmed proximal DVT or PE?
mcqs.explanation: NICE (2020): consider a DOAC for people with active cancer and confirmed proximal DVT or PE.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider a direct-acting oral anticoagulant (DOAC) for people with active cancer and confirmed proximal DVT or PE. [2020]

mcqs.question: For how long does NICE recommend anticoagulation for people with active cancer and proximal DVT or PE, before review?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: offer anticoagulation for 3 to 6 months and review at 3 to 6 months according to clinical need.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer people with active cancer and confirmed proximal DVT or PE anticoagulation treatment for 3 to 6 months. Review at 3 to 6 months according to clinical need. For recommendations on treatment after 3 to 6 months, see the section on long-term anticoagulation for secondary prevention . [2020]

mcqs.question: Anticoagulation is contraindicated in a patient with proximal DVT. What does NICE suggest?

options.A: An IVC filter, removed once anticoagulation is possible

mcqs.correctAnswerText: An IVC filter, removed once anticoagulation is possible
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider an IVC filter when anticoagulation is contraindicated; remove it once anticoagulation is no longer contraindicated and established.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider an IVC filter for people with proximal DVT or PE when anticoagulation treatment is contraindicated. Remove the IVC filter when anticoagulation treatment is no longer contraindicated and has been established. [2020]

mcqs.question: A patient with PE has haemodynamic instability. What does NICE suggest considering?

options.B: Oral DOAC alone as an outpatient

mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider pharmacological systemic thrombolytic therapy for PE with haemodynamic instability.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider pharmacological systemic thrombolytic therapy for people with PE and haemodynamic instability(see also the section on anticoagulation treatment for PE with haemodynamic instability ). [2012]

mcqs.question: Which patients with symptomatic iliofemoral DVT does NICE suggest considering for catheter-directed thrombolysis?

options.D: Symptoms <14 days, good function, life expectancy ≥1 year, low bleed risk

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Symptoms <14 days, good function, life expectancy ≥1 year, low bleed risk
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider CDT for symptomatic iliofemoral DVT with symptoms under 14 days, good functional status, life expectancy of 1 year or more and low bleeding risk.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider catheter-directed thrombolytic therapy for people with symptomatic iliofemoral DVT who have: symptoms lasting less than 14 days and good functional status and a life expectancy of 1 year or more and a low risk of bleeding. [2012] See NICE's interventional procedures guidance on ultrasound-enhanced, catheter-directed thrombolysis for deep vein thrombosis .

mcqs.question: Should anticoagulation for confirmed VTE wait for baseline blood test results, according to NICE?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not wait for baseline blood test results before starting anticoagulation.

sourceRefs.excerpt: do not wait for the results of baseline blood tests before starting anticoagulation treatment

mcqs.question: What does NICE say about hereditary thrombophilia testing in people continuing anticoagulation?

options.E: Offer it before starting a DOAC

mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not offer hereditary thrombophilia testing to people continuing anticoagulation treatment.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not offer testing for hereditary thrombophilia to people who are continuing anticoagulation treatment. [2012, amended 2020]

mcqs.question: When does NICE suggest considering hereditary thrombophilia testing?

options.B: Unprovoked VTE, first-degree relative affected, planning to stop

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Unprovoked VTE, first-degree relative affected, planning to stop
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider testing after unprovoked DVT/PE with a first-degree relative with DVT/PE if planning to stop anticoagulation; specialist advice may be needed.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider testing for hereditary thrombophilia in people who have had unprovoked DVT or PE and who have a first‑degree relative who has had DVT or PE if it is planned to stop anticoagulation treatment, but be aware that these tests can be affected by anticoagulants and specialist advice may be needed. [2012, amended 2020]

mcqs.question: When does NICE suggest testing for antiphospholipid antibodies after VTE?

options.C: At diagnosis of every provoked DVT
options.E: Unprovoked VTE when planning to stop anticoagulation

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Unprovoked VTE when planning to stop anticoagulation
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider antiphospholipid testing after unprovoked DVT/PE if planning to stop anticoagulation, noting interference from anticoagulants.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider testing for antiphospholipid antibodies in people who have had unprovoked DVT or PE if it is planned to stop anticoagulation treatment, but be aware that these tests can be affected by anticoagulants and specialist advice may be needed. [2012, amended 2020]

mcqs.question: A patient with confirmed PE weighs 135 kg. What does NICE suggest?

options.A: Anticoagulate with monitoring of therapeutic levels
options.C: Use standard dosing without any monitoring of drug levels

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Anticoagulate with monitoring of therapeutic levels
mcqs.explanation: NICE: for people under 50 kg or over 120 kg, consider anticoagulation with regular monitoring of therapeutic levels.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider anticoagulation treatment with regular monitoring of therapeutic levels for people with confirmed proximal DVT or PE who weigh less than 50 kg or more than 120 kg, to ensure effective anticoagulation. Note the cautions and requirements for dose adjustment and monitoring in the medicine's summary of product characteristics (SPC), and follow locally agreed protocols or advice from a specialist or multidisciplinary team. [2020]

mcqs.question: A patient declines continued anticoagulation after unprovoked VTE. What does NICE suggest considering?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: for people who decline continued anticoagulation, consider aspirin 75 mg or 150 mg daily (off-label in 2020).

sourceRefs.excerpt: For people who decline continued anticoagulation treatment, consider aspirin 75 mg or 150 mg daily. In March 2020, the use of aspirin for secondary prevention of DVT or PE was off label. See NICE's information on prescribing medicines . [2020]

mcqs.question: A PE patient has a 'PE unlikely' Wells score but the D-dimer result won't be available within 4 hours. What does NICE recommend?

options.E: Wait for the D-dimer without treatment

mcqs.explanation: NICE: if the D-dimer can't be obtained within 4 hours, offer interim therapeutic anticoagulation while awaiting the result.

sourceRefs.excerpt: if the D‑dimer test result cannot be obtained within 4 hours, offer interim therapeutic anticoagulation while awaiting the result (see the section on interim therapeutic anticoagulation for suspected DVT or PE ). [2012, amended 2020]

options.A: Consider VTE prophylaxis if at increased risk
options.E: Double the dose before stopping, then switch to aspirin

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Consider VTE prophylaxis if at increased risk
mcqs.explanation: NICE (2018): consider VTE prophylaxis for people at increased VTE risk who are interrupting anticoagulant therapy.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider VTE prophylaxis for people at increased risk of VTE who are interrupting anticoagulant therapy. [2018]

mcqs.question: What does NICE advise about VTE prophylaxis in people on anticoagulants for acute coronary syndrome?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: people receiving anticoagulants as part of ACS treatment don't usually need VTE prophylaxis.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Be aware that people receiving anticoagulant drugs as part of their treatment for an acute coronary syndrome do not usually need VTE prophylaxis. See also the recommendation in the section on people using anticoagulation therapy . [2018]

mcqs.question: For cardiac surgery patients not on other anticoagulation, what pharmacological VTE prophylaxis does NICE suggest considering?

options.D: Warfarin for 3 months after the plaster

mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider pharmacological prophylaxis for at least 7 days, with LMWH as first-line.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider adding pharmacological VTE prophylaxis for a minimum of 7 days for people who are undergoing cardiac surgery and are not having other anticoagulation therapy: Use LMWH as first-line treatment. If LMWH is contraindicated, use fondaparinux sodium. [2018] In March 2018, the use of LMWH and fondaparinux sodium in young people under 18 was off label. See NICE's information on prescribing medicines .

mcqs.question: Did the NICE committee recommend one DOAC over others for VTE treatment?
mcqs.explanation: The committee decided not to recommend one DOAC over the others, emphasising treatment tailored to the person.

mcqs.explanation: NICE (2019): offer enalapril postnatally with monitoring of maternal renal function and serum potassium.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer enalapril to treat hypertension in women during the postnatal period, with appropriate monitoring of maternal renal function and maternal serum potassium. [2019]

mcqs.question: After giving birth, a woman with pre-eclampsia who wasn't on antihypertensives has BP 155/102 mmHg. What does NICE advise?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: start antihypertensive treatment postnatally if BP is 150/100 mmHg or higher.

sourceRefs.excerpt: In women with pre-eclampsia who did not take antihypertensive treatment and have given birth, start antihypertensive treatment if blood pressure is 150/100 mmHg or higher. [2010]

mcqs.question: Which features of severe pre-eclampsia does NICE say should prompt consideration of magnesium sulfate?

options.E: Severe headache, scotomata, epigastric pain, rising creatinine

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Severe headache, scotomata, epigastric pain, rising creatinine
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider MgSO4 with severe headaches, visual scotomata, nausea/vomiting, epigastric pain, oliguria with severe hypertension, or deteriorating bloods (e.g. rising creatinine).

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider the need for magnesium sulfate treatment, if 1 or more of the following features of severe pre-eclampsia is present: ongoing or recurring severe headaches; visual scotomata; nausea or vomiting; epigastric pain; oliguria and severe hypertension; progressive deterioration in laboratory blood tests (such as rising creatinine or liver transaminases, or falling platelet count). [2010, amended 2019]

mcqs.question: Which drugs does NICE advise against as alternatives to magnesium sulfate in eclampsia?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not use diazepam, phenytoin or other anticonvulsants as an alternative to magnesium sulfate in eclampsia.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not use diazepam, phenytoin or other anticonvulsants as an alternative to magnesium sulfate in women with eclampsia. [2010, amended 2019]

mcqs.question: When does NICE allow volume expansion in severe pre-eclampsia?

options.C: Only if hydralazine is the antenatal antihypertensive

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Only if hydralazine is the antenatal antihypertensive
mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not use volume expansion in severe pre-eclampsia unless hydralazine is the antenatal antihypertensive.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not use volume expansion in women with severe pre-eclampsia unless hydralazine is the antenatal antihypertensive. [2010]

mcqs.question: Before low-dose epidural in severe pre-eclampsia, what does NICE say about IV fluid preload?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not preload women with severe pre-eclampsia with IV fluids before low-dose epidural or combined spinal epidural.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not preload women who have severe pre-eclampsia with intravenous fluids before establishing low-dose epidural analgesia or combined spinal epidural analgesia. [2010, amended 2019]

mcqs.question: Which test does NICE recommend to help rule out pre-eclampsia between 20 and 36+6 weeks?
mcqs.explanation: NICE (2019, amended 2023): offer PlGF-based testing to help rule out pre-eclampsia in suspected cases between 20 and 36+6 weeks.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer placental growth factor (PLGF)-based testing to help rule out pre-eclampsia in women presenting with suspected pre-eclampsia (for example, with gestational hypertension) between 20 weeks and 36 weeks and 6 days of pregnancy. (See the NICE diagnostics guidance on PLGF-based testing to help diagnose suspected preterm pre-eclampsia .) [2019, amended 2023]

mcqs.question: The urinary protein:creatinine ratio is 30 mg/mmol or above but the diagnosis of pre-eclampsia is uncertain. What does NICE suggest?

options.B: Re-test a new sample with clinical review

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Re-test a new sample with clinical review
mcqs.explanation: NICE: if the result is 30 mg/mmol or above and there's still uncertainty, consider re-testing a new sample alongside clinical review.

sourceRefs.excerpt: if the result is 30 mg/mmol or above and there is still uncertainty about the diagnosis of pre-eclampsia, consider re‑testing on a new sample, alongside clinical review. [2019]

mcqs.question: Which pregnant women does NICE say should take aspirin 75–150 mg daily from 12 weeks?

options.A: All pregnant women regardless of risk

mcqs.explanation: NICE: offer pregnant women with chronic hypertension aspirin 75 mg to 150 mg once daily from 12 weeks.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer pregnant women with chronic hypertension aspirin 75 mg to 150 mg once daily from 12 weeks. Community pharmacies cannot legally sell aspirin as a pharmacy medicine for prevention of pre-eclampsia in pregnancy in England. Aspirin for this indication must be prescribed. mcqs.question: What does NICE advise about routine thrombophilia screening after pre-eclampsia?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not routinely screen for thrombophilia in women who have had pre-eclampsia.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not routinely perform screening for thrombophilia in women who have had pre-eclampsia. [2010]

mcqs.question: Which criteria must all be met before a woman with pre-eclampsia is transferred to community care after birth, according to NICE?

options.C: Normal BP off treatment for 1 week
options.E: No symptoms, BP ≤150/100, bloods stable or improving

mcqs.correctAnswerText: No symptoms, BP ≤150/100, bloods stable or improving
mcqs.explanation: NICE: no symptoms of pre-eclampsia, BP 150/100 or less (with or without treatment), and stable or improving blood results.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer women with pre-eclampsia who have given birth transfer to community care if all of the following criteria have been met: there are no symptoms of pre-eclampsia; blood pressure, with or without treatment, is 150/100 mmHg or less; blood test results are stable or improving. [2010, amended 2019]

mcqs.question: A woman with pre-eclampsia remains on antihypertensives after transfer to community care. When does NICE recommend a review?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: offer a medical review 2 weeks after transfer to community care for women still on antihypertensive treatment.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer women who have had pre-eclampsia and who remain on antihypertensive treatment, a medical review with their GP or specialist 2 weeks after transfer to community care. [2010, amended 2019]

mcqs.question: Early birth within 7 days is likely in a woman with pre-eclampsia. What does NICE recommend?

options.A: Magnesium sulfate for all women within 24 hours

mcqs.explanation: NICE: if early birth within 7 days is likely, offer antenatal corticosteroids in line with the preterm labour guideline.

sourceRefs.excerpt: If early birth is considered likely within 7 days in women with pre-eclampsia, offer a course of antenatal corticosteroids in line with the NICE guideline on preterm labour and birth . [2010, amended 2019]

mcqs.question: What does Kidney International (2019) recommend for post-pre-eclampsia care?

options.A: Follow-up only in the next pregnancy
options.B: Defined follow-up for CV and kidney risks
options.D: Discharge at 6 weeks with no further kidney checks

mcqs.correctAnswerText: Defined follow-up for CV and kidney risks
mcqs.explanation: Post-pre-eclampsia follow-up policies should be defined to address long-term cardiovascular and kidney health risks.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Post-preeclampsia follow-up policies should be defined to address the long-term cardiovascular and kidney health risks.
