mcqs.question: How does the ATS/ERS (2013) statement describe pulmonary rehabilitation?

options.B: An optional adjunct for athletes with lung disease
options.E: A core component of chronic respiratory care

mcqs.correctAnswerText: A core component of chronic respiratory care
mcqs.explanation: ATS/ERS 2013: pulmonary rehabilitation is recognised as a core component of managing individuals with chronic respiratory disease.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Pulmonary rehabilitation is recognized as a core component of the management of individuals with chronic respiratory disease.

mcqs.question: In the 2000 randomised trial of pulmonary rehabilitation, what differed significantly between the rehabilitation and control groups?
mcqs.explanation: The number admitted didn't differ (40 vs 41), but hospital days were significantly fewer with rehabilitation (mean 10.4 vs 21.0, p=0.022).

sourceRefs.excerpt: Analysis was by intention to treat. Findings There was no difference between the rehabilitation (n=99) and control (n=101) groups in the number of patients admitted to hospital (40 vs 41) but the number of days these patients spent in hospital differed significantly (mean 10.4 [SD 9.7] vs 21.0 [20.7], p=0.022).

mcqs.question: Which addition to pulmonary rehabilitation did the 2006 study describe as feasible, possibly improving maintenance of results?

options.B: Daily oral steroids with home oxygen therapy

mcqs.explanation: A pedometer combined with exercise counselling and lifestyle activity was feasible and may improve outcome and maintenance of rehabilitation results.

sourceRefs.excerpt: The secondary outcomes showed no differences. Conclusion and practice implications This study showed that the use of the pedometer, in combination with exercise counseling and the stimulation of lifestyle physical activity, is a feasible addition to pulmonary rehabilitation which may improve outcome and maintenance of rehabilitation results.

mcqs.question: How does NICE say pulmonary rehabilitation should be organised for people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis?

options.B: Standard COPD programme only, with no adaptation

mcqs.explanation: NICE: tailor PR to the individual with IPF, at venues that are easy to get to with good disability access.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Pulmonary rehabilitation should be tailored to the individual needs of each person with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. Sessions should be held somewhere that is easy for people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis to get to and has good access for people with disabilities.

mcqs.question: Which components does NICE say pulmonary rehabilitation for IPF should include?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: offer pulmonary rehabilitation including exercise and educational components tailored to people with IPF.

sourceRefs.excerpt: If appropriate after each assessment, offer pulmonary rehabilitation including exercise and educational components tailored to the needs of people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis in general.

mcqs.question: What does NICE advise about mechanical ventilation (including NIV) for people with IPF who develop life-threatening respiratory failure?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: do not routinely offer mechanical ventilation, including NIV, to people with IPF in life-threatening respiratory failure.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Do not routinely offer mechanical ventilation (including non-invasive mechanical ventilation) to people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis who develop life-threatening respiratory failure.

mcqs.question: When does NICE suggest discussing the poor outcomes of mechanical ventilation with people with IPF?

options.D: Only on ICU admission for respiratory failure

mcqs.explanation: NICE: a respiratory physician or ILD nurse should discuss this, ideally 3–6 months after diagnosis or sooner if indicated.

sourceRefs.excerpt: A respiratory physician or specialist nurse with an interest in interstitial lung disease should discuss the poor outcomes associated with mechanical ventilation (including non-invasive mechanical ventilation) for respiratory failure with people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. These discussions should ideally take place between 3 to 6 months after diagnosis or sooner if clinically indicated. (See the recommendations in the section on best supportive care .)

mcqs.question: Smoking cessation support for people with IPF who smoke: what does NICE recommend?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: offer advice, support and treatment to aid smoking cessation to all people with IPF who smoke.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer advice, support and treatment to aid smoking cessation to all people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis who also smoke, in line with NICE's guideline on tobacco .

mcqs.question: When does NICE suggest best supportive care should start for people with IPF?

options.C: Only in the last weeks of life

mcqs.explanation: NICE: offer best supportive care from the point of diagnosis, tailored to severity, progression and preferences.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Offer best supportive care to people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis from the point of diagnosis. Best supportive care should be tailored to disease severity, rate of progression, and the person's preference, and should include if appropriate: information and support (see recommendation 1.3.1 in the section on information and support ); symptom relief; management of comorbidities; withdrawal of therapies suspected to be ineffective or causing harm; end of life care.

mcqs.question: For people with IPF and rapid disease progression, what follow-up interval does NICE suggest?
mcqs.explanation: NICE: consider follow-up every 3 months or sooner with rapid progression; every 6 months for steady progression; annually if stable after 1 year.

sourceRefs.excerpt: Consider follow-up of people with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: every 3 months or sooner if they are showing rapid disease progression or rapid deterioration of symptoms or every 6 months or sooner if they have steadily progressing disease or initially every 6 months if they have stable disease and then annually if they have stable disease after 1 year.
